edges.description: Reduced EXT2 availability compromises the EXT1/EXT2 biosynthetic complex. The founding study proposes impaired HS synthesis; complete absence of polymerization or uniformly short chains in human tissues was not measured.

Loss of available EXT2 is proposed to reduce stabilization or processing of its interacting protein NDST1. The founding cells show protein/transcript discordance, supported by independent coexpression work; the exact degradation route remains unresolved.

The founding genetic and functional study attributes the seizure-developmental syndrome to the complex EXT2 allele. This broad etiologic relation is retained with unresolved epileptogenic intermediates; the separate neural-patterning hypothesis is not treated as a demonstrated seizure circuit.

NDST1 loss is proposed to impair the sulfation component of HS biosynthesis, alongside reduced EXT2 polymerization capacity. The patient study did not directly assay sulfation; independent enzyme-expression perturbations establish that NDST1 abundance can change HS structure.

Reduced HS can alter growth-factor presentation and signaling. The human hypothesis is supported by ext2 zebrafish Fgf/Wnt perturbations; receptor-complex stability and ligand transport are alternatives, not established patient intermediates.

edges.description: Partial Ext2 loss disrupts cartilage differentiation in mice. This is retained as a qualified shared mechanism for the exostosis-positive AREXT2 family, not proof that it causes scoliosis or osteopenia in every genotype.

Reduced developmental signaling is proposed to disturb neural patterning. In fish, reduced Fgf signaling precedes abnormal midbrain-hindbrain signaling; the authors cautiously interpret this as a possible cause, not a complete reconstruction of human brain development.

edges.description: The authors explicitly connect deficient HS-dependent neural development to severe developmental delay; motor and cognitive domains are affected in the clinical reports.
The proposed disturbance of neural development provides a qualified explanation for the founding family’s cognitive impairment. It is not a measured IQ-to-pathway association.

Impaired neural development is a qualified explanation for the language component of the developmental phenotype; the source documents minimal expressive speech in the founding family but does not isolate a language-specific circuit.
The founding-study discussion explicitly links altered HS-dependent brain-size/structure development to macrocephaly. This does not explain the opposite head-size direction in the El-Bazzal family.

Abnormal cartilage differentiation is linked to ectopic bone growth in the Ext2 mouse model. The Gentile family establishes the human manifestation and proposes genotype dependence; the modeled causal route remains provisional for recessive AREXT2.
The documented seizure-associated brain injury was followed by right hemiplegia in II-4.
II-4 lost independent walking after the injury and remained wheelchair dependent; the report gives no more detailed motor-pathway localization.
Loss of a previously acquired walking skill after status-associated brain injury accounts for a motor-regression component in II-4. It does not explain all neurological regression across families.
The founding report attributes esophageal ulceration to the associated severe reflux in II-1; this is a case-specific mucosal complication.
A four-hour episode at age five caused significant brain injury in II-4; injury is a possible consequence of prolonged status, not an inevitable outcome of every seizure.
The founding report describes dysfunctional gastrointestinal motility in II-3 with easy vomiting. This clinical explanation is retained without assigning a neuronal or smooth-muscle EXT2 mechanism.

Abnormal fixation in malrotation can leave a short mesenteric attachment that permits twisting. This established anatomical route provides a qualified explanation for neonatal volvulus in II-5, who also had malrotation; his operative mesenteric anatomy was not detailed, and the EXT2-to-malrotation route remains unresolved.

Separation of the lower esophageal sphincter from the diaphragm can weaken the antireflux barrier. This supplies a plausible contribution from the documented hiatus hernia to II-1’s severe reflux. His hernia subtype, size and pressure dynamics were not measured, so the relation is qualified and does not explain reflux in siblings without documented hernia.
Immunoblotting measures reduced EXT2 abundance in cultured patient fibroblasts.
